stats.derivation: base = 100*rh_factor*spread_factor*calm_factor; rh_factor=clip((RH-70)/30,0,1); spread_factor=clip((3-S)/3,0,1), S=TMP-DPT C deg; calm_factor=clip((6-wspd)/6,0.35,1). Visibility gate only raises: VIS<1000m & RH>=95 -> >=85 (ACTIVE FOG); 1000<=VIS<5000m -> >=60. Distinct from raw visibility: calm saturated air scores high even before visibility collapses, and observed fog confirms what thermodynamics understate.

folder_html:
LIVE FOG RISK/ACTIVE FOG

A derived fog-risk index from operational HRRR analysis: low greens mark clear air, yellows and oranges mark elevated fog risk from saturated calm air, and reds into deep purple mark active fog confirmed by collapsed visibility. Built for Great Lakes navigation, shoreline conditions, aviation awareness, and nighttime environmental monitoring. Derivation: base = 100*rh_factor*spread_factor*calm_factor; rh_factor=clip((RH-70)/30,0,1); spread_factor=clip((3-S)/3,0,1), S=TMP-DPT C deg; calm_factor=clip((6-wspd)/6,0.35,1). Visibility gate only raises: VIS<1000m & RH>=95 -> >=85 (ACTIVE FOG); 1000<=VIS<5000m -> >=60. Distinct from raw visibility: calm saturated air scores high even before visibility collapses, and observed fog confirms what thermodynamics understate.

Fog science (boundary-layer meteorology and aerosol microphysics) studies saturation, radiative cooling, and droplet nucleation that reduce visibility below one kilometer. Radiation fog forms over land and calm water on clear nights; advection and steam fog form where air-water temperature contrasts drive lake-effect events. The index separates fog likelihood from raw visibility so developing risk reads before, and active fog reads during, an event.

Same index always shows the same color. Thermodynamic risk with a visibility confirmation gate — not a copy of the visibility layer.
